decks.title: Relations and Functions — Part 1: Relations and types of functions
goals: Describe a relation on a set as a set of ordered pairs
Test a relation for the reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties
Prove that a relation is an equivalence relation and find its classes
Find the domain and range of a real function
Classify a function as one-one or many-one, and onto or into

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 1
slides.body_md: Who plays the same instrument as whom? A relation records which pairs are linked.

visual.alt: Table of an imagined music club in Shillong: Ama and Banri play guitar, Daphi, Iba and Kyrsoi play drums, and Lamphrang plays the flute.
visual.caption: "Plays the same instrument as" links some members and not others.

slides.narration: Welcome to the first chapter of Class Twelve mathematics for the Indian School Certificate. Picture a small music club in Shillong. The rule plays the same instrument as links some pairs of members and not others. A rule like this is called a relation. In this part you will study relations on a set, then move on to functions and the ways we classify them.

slides.heading: What you will learn

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: relations on a set, the three properties, equivalence classes, then domain and range of functions, then one-one, onto and into functions.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Here is the route for this part. We start with relations and their three key properties, reach equivalence relations and their classes, and then study functions: where they are defined, what values they take, and whether they are one-one or onto.

slides.heading: A relation is a set of ordered pairs
slides.body_md: A **relation** $R$ on a set $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$; we write $a\,R\,b$ when $(a, b) \in R$.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation on the set 1, 2, 3 drawn with two copies of the set: 1 points to 1 and 3, 2 points to 2, and 3 points to 1 and 3.
visual.caption: $R = \{(1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 3)\}$: each arrow is one ordered pair.

slides.narration: A relation on a set A is any collection of ordered pairs taken from A cross A. In the arrow diagram, every arrow from the left copy of A to the right copy is one ordered pair. This relation has five pairs, including three loops where an element points to itself.

slides.heading: Three special relations
slides.body_md: **Empty:** no pairs. **Identity:** $I_A = \{(a, a) : a \in A\}$. **Universal:** all of $A \times A$.

visual.alt: Table of three special relations on the set p, q: the empty relation has no pairs, the identity relation has the two pairs (p, p) and (q, q), and the universal relation has all four pairs.
visual.caption: The smallest, the identity and the largest relation on $A$.

slides.narration: Three relations have names of their own. The empty relation contains no pairs at all. The identity relation contains only the loops, one for each element. The universal relation contains every possible pair. On a set with two elements these have zero, two and four pairs.

slides.heading: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive
slides.body_md: **Reflexive:** $(a, a) \in R$ for all $a$. **Symmetric:** $(a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (b, a) \in R$. **Transitive:** $(a, b), (b, c) \in R \Rightarrow (a, c) \in R$.

rows: each chain $(a, b), (b, c)$ has $(a, c)$

visual.alt: Table of how to test the three properties: reflexive needs every loop, symmetric needs each pair with its reverse, transitive needs every two-step chain closed by a shortcut; one missing item is a failure.
visual.caption: One counterexample is enough to break a property.

slides.narration: These are the three properties you will test again and again. Reflexive asks for every loop. Symmetric asks that each pair comes with its reverse. Transitive asks that any two-step chain has a one-step shortcut. To show that a property fails, a single counterexample is enough.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: test a relation
bullets: **Transitive —** chains such as $(1, 4), (4, 1)$ give $(1, 1)$ ✓; chains through loops add nothing new ✓

visual.alt: Checklist for worked example 1: reflexive yes, symmetric no because (3, 2) is missing, transitive yes.
visual.caption: Computed by testing every pair and every chain.

slides.narration: Work through the three tests in order. All four loops are present, so the relation is reflexive. The pair two comma three has no reverse, so it is not symmetric. Every chain, such as one to four and four to one, ends in a pair that is already there, so it is transitive.

slides.heading: Quick check: symmetric relations
slides.body_md: How many relations on a two-element set are symmetric?
slides.narration: Treat the loops and the off-diagonal pairs separately. Which pairs must be chosen together?

slides.heading: Equivalence relations and classes
slides.body_md: Reflexive + symmetric + transitive = **equivalence relation**. The class $[a] = \{x : x\,R\,a\}$. Classes are disjoint and cover $A$.

visual.alt: Table of the four equivalence classes of 4 divides a minus b on the numbers 1 to 10: 1, 5, 9; then 2, 6, 10; then 3, 7; then 4, 8.
visual.caption: The classes do not overlap and together make up the whole set.

slides.narration: A relation with all three properties is an equivalence relation. It sorts the set into classes of related elements. Take the rule that four divides a minus b on the numbers one to ten. The remainder on division by four decides the class, and we get four classes that never overlap.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: prove an equivalence relation
slides.body_md: On $\mathbb{Z}$, $a\,R\,b \iff 4 \mid (a + 3b)$.

nodes.label: **Transitive:** add the two conditions, then remove $4b$

visual.alt: Proof flow for worked example 2: reflexive because a plus 3 a is 4 a; symmetric by rewriting b plus 3 a; transitive by adding the two conditions and removing 4 b; so an equivalence relation.
visual.caption: Each step writes the condition as $4 \times$ an integer.

slides.narration: For a proof, use general letters, never a few numbers. Reflexive: a plus three a is four a. Symmetric: rewrite b plus three a using four times a plus b. Transitive: add the two conditions and remove four b. Each line ends with four times an integer.

slides.heading: Quick check: smallest reflexive relation
slides.body_md: How many pairs does the smallest reflexive relation on a three-element set containing one given pair have?
slides.narration: List the loops that reflexivity forces, then add the given pair.

slides.heading: Functions: domain, codomain, range
slides.body_md: A **function** $f : X \to Y$ gives each $x \in X$ exactly one image. $X$ is the domain, $Y$ the codomain, and the set of images is the **range**.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a function from X equal to u, v, w to Y equal to 1, 2, 3, 4: u and w both go to 3, v goes to 1; 2 and 4 receive no arrow.
visual.caption: Domain $X$, codomain $Y$, range $\{1, 3\}$.

slides.narration: A function is a special relation: exactly one arrow leaves each element of the domain. Elements of the codomain may receive many arrows or none. The range is the set of elements that actually receive an arrow. Here the range is just one and three.

slides.heading: Domain and range of real functions
slides.body_md: Domain: the real numbers where the formula makes sense. Range: the values the function actually takes.

visual.alt: Table of four real functions with their domains and ranges: root of x minus 3 has domain from 3 and range from 0; 1 over x minus 2 excludes 2 from the domain and 0 from the range; x squared plus 1 has range from 1; mod x minus 2 has range from minus 2.
visual.caption: Domain: where the formula makes sense. Range: the values it actually takes.

slides.narration: For a real function, the domain is decided by the formula: no negative number under a square root, no zero in a denominator. To find the range, ask which outputs are possible, often by solving y equals f of x for x, or by completing a square.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: domain and range from a graph
slides.body_md: Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \sqrt{16 - x^2}$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the square root of 16 minus x squared: the upper half of a circle of radius 4, from (minus 4, 0) up to (0, 4) and down to (4, 0).
visual.caption: Domain $[-4, 4]$, range $[0, 4]$.

slides.narration: The quantity under the root must not be negative, which gives x between minus four and four. The graph is the upper half of a circle of radius four. Its highest point is at height four and its lowest points are on the axis, so the range runs from zero to four.

slides.heading: One-one, many-one, onto, into
slides.body_md: Two independent questions: do two inputs ever share an output? Is every element of the codomain reached?

rows: no element of $Y$ gets two arrows
some output has two or more inputs
some element of $Y$ gets two arrows
every element of $Y$ gets an arrow
some element of $Y$ gets no arrow

visual.alt: Table of four types of function: one-one means different inputs give different outputs, many-one means some output is shared, onto means the range equals the codomain, into means some element of the codomain is missed.
visual.caption: Every function is one-one or many-one, and onto or into.

slides.narration: Every function answers two separate questions. If no two inputs share an output, it is one-one; otherwise many-one. If every element of the codomain is reached, it is onto; otherwise into. So a function can be one-one and into, many-one and onto, and so on.

slides.heading: The horizontal line test
slides.body_md: If some horizontal line meets the graph of $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ twice, $f$ is many-one.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 6 x, a U-shaped curve with lowest point (3, minus 9). The horizontal line y equals minus 5 cuts it at (1, minus 5) and (5, minus 5).
visual.caption: Two hits on one horizontal line: the function is many-one.

slides.narration: For real functions a graph helps. The line at height minus five cuts the curve of x squared minus six x at one and at five. Two inputs share one output, so the function is many-one. The lowest point is at minus nine, so values below that are never reached, and the function is into.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: The identity relation on a three-element set is an equivalence relation and also a function.
slides.narration: Check the three properties, then check that each element appears exactly once as a first entry.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: many-one and into
slides.body_md: Classify $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$, $f(x) = x^2 + x$.
bullets: **Into —** $x^2 + x = x(x + 1)$ is a product of consecutive integers, so it is always even; $1$ is never reached

visual.alt: Table of f of x equals x squared plus x for x from minus 2 to 2: outputs 2, 0, 0, 2, 6. The value 0 appears twice and every output is even.
visual.caption: Repeated outputs and only even values.

slides.narration: A short table of values shows the output zero twice, at minus one and at zero, so the function is many-one. Every output is even, because one of two consecutive integers is even. An odd integer such as one is never reached, so the function is into.

slides.heading: Quick check: reflexive relations
slides.body_md: Fill in the number of reflexive relations on a three-element set.
slides.narration: The three loops are compulsory. How many other pairs are free to choose?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Equivalence: reflexive, symmetric and transitive; classes partition $A$
Domain from the formula; range from the possible outputs
One-one or many-one; onto or into

visual.alt: Summary flow: a relation is a subset of A cross A; with all three properties it is an equivalence relation; a function gives one image per input; functions are one-one or many-one and onto or into.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up this part. A relation is a set of ordered pairs. With all three properties it becomes an equivalence relation, which splits the set into classes. A function has a domain, a codomain and a range, and it is either one-one or many-one, and either onto or into.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For range, solve $y = f(x)$ or complete the square
For "onto", check the pre-image lies in the **domain**

rows: reflexive 1, symmetric 1, transitive 1, each for general elements
one concrete counterexample, written as pairs

visual.alt: Exam tips table: an equivalence proof earns one mark for each property shown in general; a failed property needs one concrete counterexample; domain and range earn a mark each; one-one and onto need algebra and a counterexample for a negative answer.
visual.caption: ISC marking follows the steps, not only the final answer.

slides.narration: In the board paper, marks follow the steps. Prove each property with general letters, and use one concrete counterexample when a property fails. For a range, solve for x or complete a square. When you claim onto, always check that your pre-image lies in the domain.

decks.title: Relations and Functions — Part 2: Composite and inverse functions
goals: Form the composites f o g and g o f of algebraic functions
Show that composition is not commutative
State when a function is invertible
Find the inverse of an algebraic function, including on a restricted domain
Sketch a function and its inverse as reflections in y = x

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 2
slides.body_md: Do one function, then another; or undo a function completely.

visual.alt: Flow of a composite function: start with x, apply g to get g of x, then apply f to get f of g of x.
visual.caption: The inner function acts first.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. First we chain functions together: apply g, then apply f to the result. This is a composite function. Then we ask the reverse question: can a function be undone, and if so, how do we find the function that undoes it?

slides.heading: What you will learn

rows: decide when a function has an inverse

visual.alt: Table of the goals of Part 2: forming composites, deciding invertibility, finding inverses of algebraic functions, and sketching a function with its inverse.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Here are the goals for this part. You will form composites, decide which functions have inverses, find inverses of algebraic functions, and sketch a function together with its inverse.

slides.heading: Composite functions
slides.body_md: $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$. It is defined when the output of $g$ lies in the domain of $f$.

visual.alt: Flow of a composite function: start with x, apply g to get g of x, then apply f to get f of g of x.
visual.caption: The inner function acts first.

slides.narration: In f circle g, the inner function g acts first and f acts on its output. Read it from right to left. The composite only makes sense where the output of g is a valid input for f, so always keep an eye on the domain.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two composites
bullets: At $x = 2$: $63$ and $11$, so the composites differ

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1 with f of x equal to x squared minus 1 and g of x equal to 3 x plus 2, at x equals 0, 1 and 2: f of g gives 3, 24, 63 while g of f gives minus 1, 2, 11.
visual.caption: Different columns: $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$.

slides.narration: Substitute carefully. For f circle g, put three x plus two into f. For g circle f, put x squared minus one into g. The table compares them at three values of x, and the columns are different, so the two composites are different functions.

slides.heading: Order matters, brackets do not
slides.body_md: In general $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$, but $(f \circ g) \circ h = f \circ (g \circ h)$.

visual.alt: Table with f of x equal to 2 x, g of x equal to x plus 1 and h of x equal to x squared: f of g and g of f differ at every x shown, but the two ways of bracketing f, g and h agree.
visual.caption: Order matters; bracketing does not.

slides.narration: Composition is not commutative: changing the order usually changes the function. But composition is associative: with three functions, it does not matter how you bracket them, as long as the order stays the same. The table checks both facts at a few points.

slides.heading: Quick check: a composite value
slides.body_md: Fill in the value of a composite at one point.
slides.narration: Work from the inside out: find the inner value first.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: domain of a composite
slides.body_md: $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$ ($x \ge -1$), $g(x) = x^2 - 5$. Find $f \circ g$ and its domain.
bullets: At $x = 0$, $g(0) = -5$ is outside the domain of $f$

visual.alt: Table for worked example 2: g of x equals x squared minus 5 at minus 3, minus 2, 0, 2, 3 gives 4, minus 1, minus 5, minus 1, 4; the composite, the square root of g of x plus 1, is root 5, 0, undefined, 0, root 5.
visual.caption: At $x = 0$ the inner output $-5$ lies outside the domain of $f$.

slides.narration: The composite is the root of x squared minus four. But it only works where g of x is at least minus one, which means x squared at least four. At x equals zero the inner value is minus five, outside the domain of f, so the composite is undefined there.

slides.heading: Quick check: composing a function with itself
slides.body_md: What do you get when this rational function is composed with itself?
slides.narration: Substitute the whole function into itself and simplify the compound fraction.

slides.heading: Invertible functions
slides.body_md: $f : A \to B$ is **invertible** when there is $f^{-1} : B \to A$ with $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ and $f(f^{-1}(y)) = y$. This happens exactly when $f$ is **bijective**.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a bijection from a, b, c to 1, 2, 3: a goes to 3, b goes to 1, c goes to 2; every element of B receives exactly one arrow, so reversing the arrows gives a function.
visual.caption: Reverse every arrow of a bijection and you get $f^{-1}$.

slides.narration: A function can be undone exactly when it is a bijection. Onto guarantees that every element of B has somewhere to go back to, and one-one guarantees that there is only one place. Reverse every arrow of a bijection and you get the inverse function.

slides.heading: Finding an inverse
slides.body_md: Solve for the input in terms of the output.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps to find an inverse: check the function is a bijection, write y equals f of x, solve for x, rename to get f inverse of x, and verify by composing.
visual.caption: Five steps, the last one a check.

slides.narration: The method is always the same. Confirm the function is a bijection. Write y equals f of x and solve for x in terms of y. Then rename the variable to get f inverse of x. Finally, verify by composing: f of f inverse of x should give back x.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a linear inverse
slides.body_md: $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = \dfrac{5x - 3}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3 with f of x equal to 5 x minus 3 over 2: at x equals minus 1, 1 and 3, f gives minus 4, 1 and 6, and the inverse brings each back to minus 1, 1 and 3.
visual.caption: The inverse returns every input.

slides.narration: Clear the fraction, then isolate x. The inverse multiplies by two, adds three and divides by five, which undoes the original steps in reverse order. The table shows the inverse bringing each output back to its input.

slides.heading: Graphs of f and its inverse
slides.body_md: The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.

visual.alt: Graph of the line y equals 3 x minus 2, its inverse y equals x plus 2 over 3, and the mirror line y equals x. The two lines are reflections of each other in y equals x and all three meet at (1, 1).
visual.caption: A function and its inverse are mirror images in $y = x$.

slides.narration: If a point a comma b is on the graph of f, then b comma a is on the graph of the inverse. Swapping coordinates is a reflection in the line y equals x. Here the line y equals three x minus two and its inverse meet on the mirror line, at the point one comma one.

slides.heading: Quick check: the mirror line
slides.body_md: In which line are the graphs of a function and its inverse mirror images?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to a point when its coordinates are swapped.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: restricting the domain
bullets: On $x \ge 0$, $f$ is one-one; every $y \ge 1$ is reached

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared plus 1 for x at least 0, starting at (0, 1) and passing (2, 5), and of its inverse y equals the square root of x minus 1, starting at (1, 0) and passing (5, 2), with the mirror line y equals x between them.
visual.caption: Restricting the domain to $x \ge 0$ makes the square function invertible.

slides.narration: On all real numbers, x squared plus one is not one-one. Keep only x at least zero and it becomes a bijection onto the numbers from one upwards. Solving gives two square roots, and the domain tells you to keep the non-negative one. The two graphs mirror each other in y equals x.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a self-inverse function
slides.body_md: $f : \mathbb{R} - \{1\} \to \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$, $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x - 1}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5 with f of x equal to x plus 3 over x minus 1: f sends minus 1 to minus 1, 3 to 3 and 5 to 2, and applying f twice returns every input.
visual.caption: Here $f^{-1} = f$: the function is its own inverse.

slides.narration: Solving for x gives exactly the same formula, so this function is its own inverse. Applying it twice returns every input, as the table confirms. Notice also that the value one is excluded on both sides, which keeps the function a bijection.

slides.heading: Quick check: an inverse value
slides.body_md: Find the value of an inverse function at one point.
slides.narration: An inverse value is a pre-image: solve f of x equals the given number.

slides.heading: Properties of inverses

visual.alt: Table of properties of inverses checked with f of x equal to 2 x plus 1 and g of x equal to x cubed: the inverse of the inverse is f, the inverse of g after f is f inverse after g inverse, and f after f inverse is the identity.
visual.caption: Undo the last step first: socks and shoes.

slides.narration: Three facts are worth remembering. Inverting twice gives back the original function. To undo f followed by g, undo g first and then f, like taking off shoes before socks. And a function composed with its inverse is the identity.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ mirror in $y = x$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: a composite applies the inner function first, order matters, a function is invertible exactly when bijective, the inverse comes from solving y equals f of x, and the graphs mirror in y equals x.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. A composite applies the inner function first, and order matters. A function has an inverse exactly when it is a bijection. Find the inverse by solving for the input, and remember that the two graphs are reflections in the line y equals x.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: With a restricted domain, choose the root **using the domain**

rows: completing the square, correct root chosen, inverse with its domain
both graphs, intercepts swapped, line $y = x$

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: each composite earns a mark; invertibility needs one-one, onto and the inverse; restricted domains need completing the square and the right root; sketches need both graphs, swapped intercepts and the line y equals x.
visual.caption: Show every step; ISC awards marks for the method.

slides.narration: Some final advice. Write each composite in full before simplifying. Before writing an inverse, state that the function is one-one and onto. On a restricted domain, let the domain decide which root to keep. And never confuse the inverse function with the reciprocal of the function.

notes.title: Relations and Functions — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Relations on a set
sections.body_md:
A **relation** on $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$. If $n(A) = n$, there are $n^2$ ordered pairs and $2^{n^2}$ relations.

- **Empty relation:** $\varnothing$. **Universal relation:** $A \times A$. **Identity relation:** $I_A = \{(a, a) : a \in A\}$.

visual.alt: Table of three special relations on the set p, q: the empty relation has no pairs, the identity relation has the two pairs (p, p) and (q, q), and the universal relation has all four pairs.
visual.caption: The smallest, the identity and the largest relation on $A$.

sections.heading: 2. Reflexive, symmetric, transitive and equivalence relations
sections.body_md:
- **Reflexive:** $(a, a) \in R$ for every $a \in A$.
- **Symmetric:** $(a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (b, a) \in R$.
- **Transitive:** $(a, b) \in R,\ (b, c) \in R \Rightarrow (a, c) \in R$.

All three together make an **equivalence relation**. Its classes $[a] = \{x \in A : x\,R\,a\}$ are disjoint and cover $A$ (a partition). "Same value of a property" (same remainder, same instrument) always gives an equivalence relation.

To prove a property, use general letters; to disprove one, give one concrete counterexample.

rows: each chain $(a, b), (b, c)$ has $(a, c)$

visual.alt: Table of how to test the three properties: reflexive needs every loop, symmetric needs each pair with its reverse, transitive needs every two-step chain closed by a shortcut; one missing item is a failure.
visual.caption: One counterexample is enough to break a property.

visuals.alt: Table of the four equivalence classes of 4 divides a minus b on the numbers 1 to 10: 1, 5, 9; then 2, 6, 10; then 3, 7; then 4, 8.
visuals.caption: The classes do not overlap and together make up the whole set.

sections.heading: 3. Functions, domain and range
sections.body_md:
A **function** $f : X \to Y$ assigns to each $x \in X$ exactly one $f(x) \in Y$. **Domain** $X$, **codomain** $Y$, **range** $\{f(x) : x \in X\} \subseteq Y$.

For real functions: exclude values that make a denominator zero or put a negative number under an even root. Find the range by solving $y = f(x)$ for $x$ or by completing the square (for example $x^2 - 4x + 9 = (x - 2)^2 + 5 \ge 5$).

key_terms.definition_md: The set of values the function actually takes.

visual.alt: Table of four real functions with their domains and ranges: root of x minus 3 has domain from 3 and range from 0; 1 over x minus 2 excludes 2 from the domain and 0 from the range; x squared plus 1 has range from 1; mod x minus 2 has range from minus 2.
visual.caption: Domain: where the formula makes sense. Range: the values it actually takes.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals the square root of 16 minus x squared: the upper half of a circle of radius 4, from (minus 4, 0) up to (0, 4) and down to (4, 0).
visuals.caption: Domain $[-4, 4]$, range $[0, 4]$.

sections.heading: 4. One-one, many-one, onto and into functions
sections.body_md:
- **One-one:** $f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$. Otherwise **many-one**.
- **Onto:** every $y \in Y$ has a pre-image (range $= Y$). Otherwise **into**.
- **Bijective:** one-one and onto.

Finite sets with $n(X) = m$, $n(Y) = n$: $n^m$ functions; $n(n - 1)\cdots(n - m + 1)$ one-one functions when $m \le n$; onto functions to a $2$-element set: $2^m - 2$. A horizontal line meeting a graph twice shows "many-one".

key_terms.definition_md: A function whose range is smaller than its codomain.
Some output has two or more pre-images.

rows: no element of $Y$ gets two arrows
some output has two or more inputs
some element of $Y$ gets two arrows
every element of $Y$ gets an arrow
some element of $Y$ gets no arrow

visual.alt: Table of four types of function: one-one means different inputs give different outputs, many-one means some output is shared, onto means the range equals the codomain, into means some element of the codomain is missed.
visual.caption: Every function is one-one or many-one, and onto or into.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 6 x, a U-shaped curve with lowest point (3, minus 9). The horizontal line y equals minus 5 cuts it at (1, minus 5) and (5, minus 5).
visuals.caption: Two hits on one horizontal line: the function is many-one.

sections.heading: 5. Composite functions
sections.body_md:
$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first. It needs the range of $g$ to lie in the domain of $f$ (restrict $x$ where necessary).

- Not commutative: usually $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$.
- Associative: $(f \circ g) \circ h = f \circ (g \circ h)$.
- Composites of one-one functions are one-one; composites of onto functions are onto.

ISC 2027 asks for composites of **algebraic** functions only.

visual.alt: Flow of a composite function: start with x, apply g to get g of x, then apply f to get f of g of x.

sections.heading: 6. Invertible functions and their graphs
sections.body_md:
$f : A \to B$ is **invertible** exactly when it is **bijective**; then $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$.

Method: check one-one and onto, write $y = f(x)$, solve for $x$, rename, and verify $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$. On a restricted domain (for example $x \ge 0$), the domain decides which root to keep.

The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in $y = x$; a point where they meet lies on $y = x$. Also $(f^{-1})^{-1} = f$ and $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$. Note that $f^{-1}(x)$ is not $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Equivalence proof (3 marks):* one mark each for reflexive, symmetric and transitive, using general letters; classes earn further marks when asked.
- *Property fails (1–2 marks):* one explicit counterexample.
- *Domain and range (2 marks):* one each, with the reason.
- *Invertible and inverse (2–3 marks):* one-one, onto, then the inverse; check by composing.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading $f \circ g$ as "$f$ first".
- Writing $f^{-1}$ before showing $f$ is a bijection.
- Keeping both roots on a restricted domain.
- Forgetting the excluded value in the codomain of a rational function.

questions.stem_md: Which condition must hold for a relation $R$ on a set $A$ to be called **transitive**?

options.text_md: $(a, b) \in R$ and $(b, c) \in R$ imply $(a, c) \in R$

questions.solution_md: Transitivity is the "two steps force a shortcut" rule. (b) defines symmetric, (c) reflexive, and (d) describes an asymmetric relation.

questions.stem_md: On the set of letters $L = \{p, q, r\}$, the relation $R = \{(p, p), (q, q), (r, r), (p, q), (q, p)\}$ is

options.text_md: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive

questions.solution_md: All three loops are present, every pair comes with its reverse, and the only chains, $(p, q), (q, p)$ and $(q, p), (p, q)$, give loops that are present. So $R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

questions.stem_md: A two-element set $\{1, 2\}$ is given. Counting by pairs on and off the diagonal, how many of the relations on it are **symmetric**?
questions.solution_md: The two loops $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$ may each be in or out ($2^2$ ways); the pair $(1, 2)$, $(2, 1)$ must go in or out together ($2$ ways): $2^2 \times 2 = 8$.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined geometry notebook, $T$ is the set of all triangles drawn, and $\Delta_1\,R\,\Delta_2$ means "$\Delta_1$ is similar to $\Delta_2$". The relation $R$ is
questions.solution_md: Every triangle is similar to itself; similarity works both ways; and two triangles similar to a third are similar to each other (equal angles pass along). So $R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

questions.stem_md: For the relation "the difference is a multiple of $5$" on the integers, which set is the class $[2]$?
questions.solution_md: $b \in [2]$ exactly when $b - 2 = 5k$, i.e. $b = 5k + 2$: $\{\dots, -8, -3, 2, 7, 12, \dots\}$. Option (d) is the class of $3$.

questions.stem_md: On the set $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 12\}$, a stamp collector writes $a\,R\,b$ when $b$ is a multiple of $a$. The relation $R$ is

options.text_md: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
reflexive and transitive but not symmetric

questions.solution_md: $a$ is a multiple of itself (reflexive). If $b = ma$ and $c = nb$ then $c = mna$ (transitive). But $2\,R\,4$ while $4$ does not divide $2$ (not symmetric).

questions.stem_md: On $\{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$, $a\,R\,b$ holds when $4$ divides $a - b$. Into how many equivalence classes does $R$ split the set?
questions.solution_md: The classes follow the remainder on division by $4$: $\{1, 5, 9\}$, $\{2, 6, 10\}$, $\{3, 7\}$, $\{4, 8\}$, so $4$ classes.

questions.stem_md: What is the number of ordered pairs in the smallest **reflexive** relation on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ that already contains the pair $(1, 2)$?
questions.solution_md: Reflexivity forces the three loops $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$, $(3, 3)$; adding the given $(1, 2)$ gives $4$ pairs. Nothing else is forced.

questions.stem_md: On $\{1, 2, 3\}$ the relation $\{(1, 2), (2, 3)\}$ is not transitive. Adding which **single** pair makes it transitive?
questions.solution_md: The chain $(1, 2), (2, 3)$ demands $(1, 3)$. Adding $(3, 1)$ creates a new chain $(2, 3), (3, 1)$ needing $(2, 1)$; adding $(2, 1)$ creates $(1, 2), (2, 1)$ needing $(1, 1)$; adding $(1, 1)$ leaves $(1, 3)$ missing.

questions.stem_md: What is the largest set of real numbers on which $f(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^2}$ takes real values?
questions.solution_md: We need $9 - x^2 \ge 0$, i.e. $x^2 \le 9$, i.e. $-3 \le x \le 3$. The end points are allowed because $\sqrt 0 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: A real function is given by $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 4}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Its range is
questions.solution_md: $x^2 + 4 \ge 4$, so $0 < f(x) \le \dfrac14$, with $\dfrac14$ reached at $x = 0$. The value $0$ is never reached because the denominator is finite.

questions.stem_md: Which of these functions from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is **many-one**?
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - 6x$ takes the value $0$ at both $x = 0$ and $x = 6$, so two inputs share an image. The other three are one-one.

questions.stem_md: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 5$, is
questions.solution_md: $f(x) = (x + 1)^2 + 4$, so $f(-3) = f(1) = 8$ (not one-one), and every value is at least $4$, so $0$ has no pre-image (not onto).

questions.stem_md: How many functions from the four-element set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ onto the two-element set $\{a, b\}$ are there?
questions.solution_md: There are $2^4 = 16$ functions in all, and only the two constant ones miss an element: $16 - 2 = 14$.

questions.stem_md: From a three-element set to a four-element set, how many functions are **into** (that is, not onto)?
questions.solution_md: Three inputs can reach at most three of the four elements, so no function is onto: all $4^3 = 64$ functions are into.

questions.stem_md: The function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $f(n) = n^2$, is
questions.solution_md: Squares of different natural numbers differ (one-one), but $2$, $3$, $5$, … are not squares (into, not onto).

questions.stem_md: With $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = 2x - 3$, the value of $(f \circ g)(2)$ is
questions.solution_md: $(f \circ g)(2) = f(g(2)) = f(1) = 1^2 + 1 = 2$. The value $7$ is $(g \circ f)(2) = g(5)$: the order matters.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = 3x + 2$ and $g(x) = \dfrac{x}{3}$, the composite $(g \circ f)(x)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $(g \circ f)(x) = g(3x + 2) = \dfrac{3x + 2}{3} = x + \dfrac23$. Note $(f \circ g)(x) = 3 \cdot \dfrac x3 + 2 = x + 2$, which is option (c).

questions.stem_md: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x - 1}$ for $x \ne 1$. Composing $f$ with itself gives $(f \circ f)(x) =$
questions.solution_md: $f(f(x)) = \dfrac{\frac{x}{x - 1}}{\frac{x}{x - 1} - 1} = \dfrac{\frac{x}{x - 1}}{\frac{1}{x - 1}} = x$. So $f$ undoes itself.

questions.stem_md: Take $f(x) = x + 4$ and $g(x) = x^2$. By how much does $(g \circ f)(-1)$ exceed $(f \circ g)(-1)$?
questions.solution_md: $(g \circ f)(-1) = g(3) = 9$ and $(f \circ g)(-1) = f(1) = 5$; the difference is $9 - 5 = 4$, so $g \circ f \ne f \circ g$.

questions.stem_md: The bijection $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = \dfrac{2x - 5}{3}$, has inverse
questions.solution_md: Put $y = \dfrac{2x - 5}{3}$: $3y = 2x - 5$, so $x = \dfrac{3y + 5}{2}$. Hence $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 5}{2}$. Note that $\dfrac{3}{2x - 5}$ is a reciprocal, not an inverse.

questions.stem_md: The function $f : [0, \infty) \to [3, \infty)$, $f(x) = x^2 + 3$, is a bijection. Its inverse $f^{-1}(x)$, for $x \ge 3$, is
questions.solution_md: $y = x^2 + 3$ gives $x^2 = y - 3$, and $x \ge 0$ picks the non-negative root: $x = \sqrt{y - 3}$. The negative root is outside the domain $[0, \infty)$.

questions.stem_md: A function $f : A \to B$ has an inverse function $f^{-1} : B \to A$ exactly when $f$ is
questions.solution_md: $f^{-1}$ must send each $y \in B$ to exactly one $x$: onto gives at least one pre-image, one-one gives at most one. Both are needed.

questions.stem_md: The map $f : \mathbb{R} - \{2\} \to \mathbb{R} - \{4\}$ given by $f(x) = \dfrac{4x + 1}{x - 2}$ is invertible. Its inverse is
questions.solution_md: $y(x - 2) = 4x + 1 \Rightarrow xy - 4x = 2y + 1 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{2y + 1}{y - 4}$. So $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 4}$, defined for $x \ne 4$.

questions.stem_md: On one set of axes, the graph of an invertible function and the graph of its inverse are mirror images in the line
questions.solution_md: $(a, b)$ lies on the graph of $f$ exactly when $(b, a)$ lies on the graph of $f^{-1}$, and swapping coordinates is reflection in $y = x$.

questions.stem_md: For the bijection $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = x^3 - 2$, the value of $f^{-1}(6)$ is
questions.solution_md: $f^{-1}(6)$ is the $x$ with $x^3 - 2 = 6$, so $x^3 = 8$ and $x = 2$. The value $214 = f(6)$ is the trap.

questions.stem_md: If two functions are both one-one, then their composite (where defined) is also one-one.
questions.solution_md: If $f(g(x_1)) = f(g(x_2))$, one-one $f$ gives $g(x_1) = g(x_2)$, and one-one $g$ gives $x_1 = x_2$.

questions.stem_md: Every many-one function is an into function.
questions.solution_md: $f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty)$, $f(x) = x^2$, is many-one ($f(-1) = f(1)$) and yet onto: every $y \ge 0$ is $(\sqrt y)^2$.

questions.stem_md: On $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the identity relation $\{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)\}$ is an equivalence relation and also a function from $A$ to $A$.
questions.solution_md: It is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; and each element appears exactly once as a first entry, so it is a function (the identity function).

questions.stem_md: Every relation on a three-element set that contains all three loops $(a, a)$ is reflexive. The number of such reflexive relations is ____.
questions.solution_md: The $3$ loops are forced; each of the other $6$ pairs is free: $2^6 = 64$.

questions.stem_md: If $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, then $(g \circ f)(1) =$ ____.
The least number in the range of $f(x) = |x - 2| + 3$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, is ____.
questions.solution_md: $|x - 2| \ge 0$ with equality at $x = 2$, so the least value is $0 + 3 = 3$.

questions.stem_md: If $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, then $f^{-1}(x) =$ ____ (write it in the form $ax + b$).
questions.solution_md: $y = \dfrac{x + 3}{2} \Rightarrow x = 2y - 3$, so $f^{-1}(x) = 2x - 3$.

questions.stem_md: On the four-letter set $\{a, b, c, d\}$, how many equivalence relations contain the pair $(a, b)$?
questions.solution_md: Such a relation puts $a$ and $b$ in one class. Treat $\{a, b\}$ as one object; the ways to split the three objects $\{a, b\}$, $c$, $d$ into classes are $5$.

questions.stem_md: How many one-one functions are there from $\{x, y, z\}$ to a set of $5$ elements?
questions.solution_md: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$.

questions.stem_md: Let $f(x) = 3x - 4$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$. Find $(f \circ g)(2) - (g \circ f)(2)$.
For the bijection $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 7}{3}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, find $f^{-1}(5)$.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{x + 7}{3} = 5 \Rightarrow x = 8$.

questions.stem_md: Find the least element of the range of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 9$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
questions.solution_md: $f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 5 \ge 5$, with equality at $x = 2$: least value $5$.

questions.stem_md: On $\{1, 2, \dots, 8\}$, $a\,R\,b$ whenever $a - b$ is a multiple of $3$. How many ordered pairs belong to $R$?
A quiz master pairs the numbered cards $1$ to $6$ by the rule $a\,R\,b$ if and only if $a + b$ is even. Show that $R$ is symmetric and write the equivalence class $[2]$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Symmetric:** $a + b = b + a$, so if $a + b$ is even, so is $b + a$; hence $a\,R\,b \Rightarrow b\,R\,a$.

**Class:** $b \in [2]$ when $2 + b$ is even, i.e. $b$ is even: $[2] = \{2, 4, 6\}$.

questions.solution_md: Use a + b = b + a; then list the cards with the same parity as 2.

questions.stem_md: Write down a relation on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ that is symmetric and transitive but **not** reflexive, and say which pair is missing for reflexivity.

answer.model_answer_md: Take $R = \{(1, 1), (2, 2)\}$ (or the empty relation). Every pair is its own reverse, so $R$ is symmetric; every chain ends in a loop already present, so it is transitive. It is not reflexive because $(3, 3) \notin R$.

questions.solution_md: Any symmetric, transitive relation that leaves out at least one loop.

questions.stem_md: Find the domain and the range of the real function $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Domain:** $x - 3 \ge 0$, so $x \ge 3$: domain $[3, \infty)$.

**Range:** the square root takes every non-negative value ($f(3 + t^2) = t$ for $t \ge 0$) and no negative value: range $[0, \infty)$.

questions.solution_md: Radicand non-negative; then ask which outputs occur.

questions.stem_md: A ticket machine prints the number $f(n) = 3n + 2$ for the $n$th customer, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, as a map $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. Show that $f$ is one-one but not onto.

answer.model_answer_md:
**One-one:** $3n_1 + 2 = 3n_2 + 2 \Rightarrow n_1 = n_2$.

**Not onto:** every output is at least $5$, so $1$ (and also $6$, which is not of the form $3n + 2$) has no pre-image in $\mathbb{N}$.

questions.solution_md: Cancel for one-one; exhibit a natural number that is never printed.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 5$ on $\mathbb{R}$, write $(f \circ g)(x)$ and $(g \circ f)(x)$, and give one value of $x$ that shows they are different functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
$(f \circ g)(x) = f(x + 5) = (x + 5)^2$ and $(g \circ f)(x) = g(x^2) = x^2 + 5$.

At $x = 0$: $(f \circ g)(0) = 25$ but $(g \circ f)(0) = 5$, so $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute in the right order, then compare at a convenient point.

e -1$, simplify $(f \circ f)(x)$ (for $x 
e 0$, $x

questions.solution_md: Combine the numerator and the denominator over x + 1 before dividing.

questions.stem_md: A delivery app charges a rider a penalty score $f(x) = 7 - 4x$ that is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and verify that $f\left(f^{-1}(x)\right) = x$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$y = 7 - 4x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{7 - y}{4}$, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{7 - x}{4}$.

Check: $f\left(\dfrac{7 - x}{4}\right) = 7 - (7 - x) = x$.

questions.solution_md: Solve y = 7 − 4x for x, then substitute back.

questions.stem_md: Show that $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = x^3 + 5$, is invertible and write $f^{-1}(x)$.

answer.model_answer_md: **One-one:** $x_1^3 + 5 = x_2^3 + 5 \Rightarrow x_1^3 = x_2^3 \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$. **Onto:** for any real $y$, $x = \sqrt[3]{y - 5}$ gives $f(x) = y$. So $f$ is a bijection, hence invertible, with $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 5}$.

questions.solution_md: Bijective implies invertible; solve y = x³ + 5 for x.

questions.stem_md: Find the domain and the range of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Domain:** the denominator must not vanish: $\mathbb{R} - \{2\}$.

**Range:** $y = \dfrac{1}{x - 2} \Rightarrow x = 2 + \dfrac1y$, possible for every $y \ne 0$, and $y = 0$ never occurs: range $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

questions.solution_md: Solve for x in terms of y to see which outputs occur.

questions.stem_md: On $\mathbb{Z}$, define $a\,R\,b$ if and only if $3a + 4b$ is divisible by $7$. Prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Reflexive:** $3a + 4a = 7a$, divisible by $7$.

**Symmetric:** if $3a + 4b = 7k$, then $3b + 4a = 7(a + b) - (3a + 4b) = 7(a + b - k)$, divisible by $7$.

**Transitive:** if $3a + 4b = 7k$ and $3b + 4c = 7m$, adding gives $3a + 7b + 4c = 7(k + m)$, so $3a + 4c = 7(k + m - b)$.

Hence $R$ is an equivalence relation.

questions.solution_md: Rewrite each condition as 7 times an integer.

questions.stem_md: A school fair sells raffle tickets numbered $1$ to $20$. Two tickets are related when their numbers end in the same digit. Explain why this is an equivalence relation, write the class of ticket $13$, and state how many classes there are.

answer.model_answer_md:
"Same last digit" is equality of one property of the number, so the relation is reflexive (same as itself), symmetric (equality works both ways) and transitive (equal to equal is equal).

Class of $13$: tickets ending in $3$, i.e. $\{3, 13\}$.

The last digit can be any of $0, 1, \dots, 9$, so there are $10$ classes.

questions.solution_md: Equality of a property always gives an equivalence relation.

questions.stem_md: Decide, with reasons, whether $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = x\,|x|$, is one-one and whether it is onto.

answer.model_answer_md:
$f(x) = x^2$ for $x \ge 0$ and $f(x) = -x^2$ for $x < 0$.

**One-one:** outputs of non-negative inputs are $\ge 0$ and of negative inputs are $< 0$, so equal outputs come from inputs of the same sign; on each part $x^2$ (or $-x^2$) is one-one there. Hence $f$ is one-one.

**Onto:** for $y \ge 0$ take $x = \sqrt{y}$; for $y < 0$ take $x = -\sqrt{-y}$. Every real $y$ is reached, so $f$ is onto — a bijection.

questions.solution_md: Split by the sign of x.

questions.stem_md: Is $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{1 + x^2}$, one-one? Is it onto? Justify both answers.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Not one-one:** $f(-1) = f(1) = \dfrac12$.

**Not onto:** $0 \le x^2 < 1 + x^2$, so $0 \le f(x) < 1$ for every real $x$. A number such as $2$ (or $-1$) in the codomain has no pre-image. The range is $[0, 1)$.

questions.solution_md: An even function repeats values; bound the fraction for onto.

questions.stem_md: Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ for $x \ge 0$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 1$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Find $(f \circ g)(x)$ and its domain, and find $(g \circ f)(x)$ for $x \ge 0$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$(f \circ g)(x) = f(x^2 - 1) = \sqrt{x^2 - 1}$, defined when $x^2 - 1 \ge 0$, i.e. $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$: domain $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.

$(g \circ f)(x) = g(\sqrt x) = (\sqrt x)^2 - 1 = x - 1$ for $x \ge 0$.

questions.solution_md: The inner output must lie in the domain of the outer function.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = 2x + 3$ and $g(x) = \dfrac{x - 3}{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, show that $f \circ g$ and $g \circ f$ are both the identity function, and state what this says about $f$ and $g$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$(f \circ g)(x) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{x - 3}{2} + 3 = x$ and $(g \circ f)(x) = \dfrac{(2x + 3) - 3}{2} = x$.

Both composites are the identity on $\mathbb{R}$, so $f$ and $g$ are inverses of each other: $g = f^{-1}$ and $f = g^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Two-sided identity composites characterise inverse functions.

questions.stem_md: Show that $f : \mathbb{R} - \{-1\} \to \mathbb{R} - \{2\}$, $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 3}{x + 1}$, is invertible, and find $f^{-1}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Values avoid $2$:** $\dfrac{2x + 3}{x + 1} = 2$ would give $2x + 3 = 2x + 2$, impossible.

**Solve $y = f(x)$:** $y(x + 1) = 2x + 3 \Rightarrow x(y - 2) = 3 - y \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{3 - y}{y - 2}$, a unique $x$ (and $x \ne -1$, because setting $3 - y = -(y - 2)$ leads to a false statement). So $f$ is one-one and onto, hence invertible.

$f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3 - x}{x - 2}$, $x \ne 2$.

questions.solution_md: A unique solution x for every y in the codomain proves one-one and onto together.

questions.stem_md: The function $f : [1, \infty) \to [-2, \infty)$ is $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 1$. Show that it is a bijection and find $f^{-1}(x)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$f(x) = (x - 1)^2 - 2$.

**One-one:** for $x \ge 1$, $x - 1 \ge 0$, and $(x_1 - 1)^2 = (x_2 - 1)^2$ with both bases non-negative gives $x_1 = x_2$.

**Onto and inverse:** for $y \ge -2$, $(x - 1)^2 = y + 2 \Rightarrow x = 1 + \sqrt{y + 2} \ge 1$. So every $y$ is reached and $f^{-1}(x) = 1 + \sqrt{x + 2}$.

questions.solution_md: Complete the square; the restricted domain picks the positive root.

questions.stem_md: A canteen assigns each of $4$ snack trays to one of $3$ counters. Treating each assignment as a function from the trays to the counters, find (i) the number of all such functions, (ii) how many are onto, (iii) how many are one-one.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Each tray has $3$ choices: $3^4 = 81$.

(ii) Onto: one counter gets two trays. Choose the two trays sharing a counter in $\binom42 = 6$ ways and assign the three groups to the counters in $3! = 6$ ways: $36$.

(iii) One-one needs $4$ different counters out of $3$: impossible, so $0$.

questions.solution_md: Count all, then count by grouping for onto; pigeonhole for one-one.

questions.stem_md: For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = 2x - 4$, find $f^{-1}$, describe how the two graphs are placed on one set of axes, and find the point where they meet.

answer.model_answer_md:
$y = 2x - 4 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{y + 4}{2}$, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 4}{2}$.

The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the mirror image of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$ (the $y$-intercept $-4$ of $f$ becomes the $x$-intercept $-4$ of $f^{-1}$).

They meet where $2x - 4 = \dfrac{x + 4}{2}$, i.e. $4x - 8 = x + 4$, $x = 4$: the point $(4, 4)$, which lies on $y = x$.

questions.solution_md: Reflection in y = x; solve f(x) = f⁻¹(x).

questions.stem_md:
On $\mathbb{Z}$, define $a\,R\,b$ if and only if $a^2 - b^2$ is divisible by $5$.

(a) Prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation. [3]

(b) Restrict $R$ to $A = \{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$ and write the class $[1]$ and the class $[5]$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Reflexive:** $a^2 - a^2 = 0 = 5 \times 0$.

**Symmetric:** if $a^2 - b^2 = 5k$, then $b^2 - a^2 = 5(-k)$.

**Transitive:** if $a^2 - b^2 = 5k$ and $b^2 - c^2 = 5m$, adding gives $a^2 - c^2 = 5(k + m)$.

So $R$ is an equivalence relation.

**(b)** Squares leave remainder $1$ on division by $5$ for $a = 1, 4, 6, 9$ and remainder $0$ for $a = 5, 10$. So $[1] = \{1, 4, 6, 9\}$ and $[5] = \{5, 10\}$.

questions.solution_md: Write each difference of squares as 5 times an integer; group by the remainder of a².

questions.stem_md:
A function maps the reals other than $2$ to the reals other than $3$ by $f(x) = \dfrac{3x - 1}{x - 2}$.

(a) Prove that equal outputs force equal inputs. [2]

(b) Prove that every element of the codomain is attained, giving its pre-image, and conclude that $f$ is a bijection. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Let $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$: $(3x_1 - 1)(x_2 - 2) = (3x_2 - 1)(x_1 - 2)$.

$3x_1x_2 - 6x_1 - x_2 + 2 = 3x_1x_2 - 6x_2 - x_1 + 2 \Rightarrow -5x_1 = -5x_2 \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$. So $f$ is one-one.

**(b)** Outputs avoid $3$: $\dfrac{3x - 1}{x - 2} = 3$ gives $3x - 1 = 3x - 6$, impossible.

For $y \ne 3$: $y(x - 2) = 3x - 1 \Rightarrow x(y - 3) = 2y - 1 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{2y - 1}{y - 3}$, defined since $y \ne 3$, and $x \ne 2$ (that would need $2y - 1 = 2y - 6$).

So every $y$ in the codomain has the pre-image $\dfrac{2y - 1}{y - 3}$: $f$ is onto, and with (a) a bijection.

questions.solution_md: Cross-multiply for one-one; solve for x and check both excluded values for onto.

questions.stem_md:
Let $f(x) = x + 3$ and $g(x) = 2x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

(a) Find $(f \circ g)(x)$ and $(g \circ f)(x)$. [2]

(b) Find every real $x$ for which $(f \circ g)(x) = (g \circ f)(x)$, and check your answer. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $(f \circ g)(x) = f(2x^2) = 2x^2 + 3$; $(g \circ f)(x) = g(x + 3) = 2(x + 3)^2 = 2x^2 + 12x + 18$.

**(b)** $2x^2 + 3 = 2x^2 + 12x + 18 \Rightarrow 12x = -15 \Rightarrow x = -\dfrac54$.

Check: $(f \circ g)\left(-\dfrac54\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{25}{16} + 3 = \dfrac{49}{8}$ and $(g \circ f)\left(-\dfrac54\right) = 2\left(\dfrac74\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{8}$. Equal, so $x = -\dfrac54$ is the only solution.

questions.solution_md: Expand, cancel the x² terms, solve the linear equation.

questions.stem_md:
Consider $f : [-2, \infty) \to [-5, \infty)$, $f(x) = x^2 + 4x - 1$.

(a) Show that $f$ is one-one and onto. [2]

(b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [2]

(c) Find $f^{-1}(4)$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
$f(x) = (x + 2)^2 - 5$.

**(a)** For $x \ge -2$, $x + 2 \ge 0$; equal squares of non-negative numbers have equal bases, so $f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$. For $y \ge -5$, $x = -2 + \sqrt{y + 5} \ge -2$ gives $f(x) = y$, so $f$ is onto.

**(b)** From $(x + 2)^2 = y + 5$ and $x + 2 \ge 0$: $f^{-1}(x) = -2 + \sqrt{x + 5}$, $x \ge -5$.

**(c)** $f^{-1}(4) = -2 + \sqrt{9} = 1$ (check: $f(1) = 1 + 4 - 1 = 4$).

questions.solution_md: Complete the square; the domain restriction selects the positive root.

questions.stem_md:
A real function is $f(x) = 3x - 6$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

(a) Show that $f$ is invertible and find $f^{-1}$. [2]

(b) Sketch $f$ and $f^{-1}$ on the same axes, marking their intercepts, and explain why they meet on the line $y = x$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $3x_1 - 6 = 3x_2 - 6 \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$ (one-one); for any $y$, $x = \dfrac{y + 6}{3}$ works (onto). So $f$ is invertible with $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 6}{3}$.

**(b)** $f$: a line through $(2, 0)$ and $(0, -6)$. $f^{-1}$: a line through $(-6, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$ — each intercept of $f$ appears with coordinates swapped.

The graphs are reflections of each other in $y = x$, so any meeting point is its own reflection, i.e. lies on $y = x$. Solving $3x - 6 = x$ gives $x = 3$: they meet at $(3, 3)$.

questions.solution_md: Swap coordinates for the inverse graph; a fixed point of reflection lies on the mirror.
